title: Sub-microsecond conformational dynamics in an optical nanocavity
authors: Heehun Sung, Sam C Scholten, Pavlina Sasheva, Igor Marinkovic, Warwick P Bowen
abstract: Microsecond conformational changes underlie many protein functions, but ensemble averaging has been needed to observe them without labels. Single-shot measurements on individual proteins have had insufficient speed, while protein Brownian-motion has obscured signals. Here, we report a fibre-integrated silicon-photonic sensor that overcomes these barriers, resolving protein dynamics at sub-microsecond speeds in continuous single-shot measurements that can extend over minutes. This is achieved by combining far-sub-wavelength optical field confinement with high optical field uniformity that suppresses protein Brownian-motion by a factor of sixty. In single-shot measurements on ferritin molecules, we observe tens of thousands of transitions consistent with conformational fluctuations of the ferritin shell, resolving them over timescales as short as 400 ns. The ability to continuously monitor transitions over long times reveals switching kinetics, memory effects and molecular heterogeneity hidden in ensemble averages. This opens a new path to improved mechanistic understanding of protein function.
summary: The researchers developed and employed a novel silicon-photonic nanocavity sensor capable of monitoring single protein dynamics at sub-microsecond resolution. By measuring minute shifts in the optical resonance frequency upon conformational change, they resolved complex kinetic pathways in ferritin that were previously obscured by noise or ensemble averaging. This work establishes a powerful new tool for understanding fundamental biophysical processes.
main_problem: Observing protein conformational dynamics occurring on microsecond timescales is challenging due to limitations in measurement speed, Brownian motion noise, and the need for label-free techniques.
main_result: The authors successfully resolved tens of thousands of transitions in ferritin over sub-microsecond timescales using a novel photonic sensor, revealing hidden kinetic details like switching kinetics and memory effects.
method: They utilized a fibre-integrated silicon-photonic nanocavity to measure the resonance frequency shift caused by protein binding, achieving high temporal resolution while suppressing Brownian motion noise.
model_or_system: The system is a slot photonic crystal cavity fabricated on silicon, used as a single-molecule sensor. The dynamics are analyzed using Hidden Markov Models (HMM) and potential energy landscape derivations from probability distributions.
key_observables: Cavity resonance frequency shift ($\delta\omega$), Power Spectral Density (PSD), double-well potential shape, transition stepping events, and Mean Squared Displacements (MSDs).
important_parameters: Sub-microsecond resolution, Brownian motion suppression factor of sixty, ionic strength (NaCl concentration) for tuning dynamics.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that the observed fluctuations can be mapped to an effective potential energy landscape via the Boltzmann relation; transition path time calculations assume low energy barriers.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the photonic crystal structure and setup, show ferritin monolayer formation and signal stabilization, track fast motions revealing a bimodal potential, and demonstrate stepping dynamics tunable by ionic strength.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the physical sensor platform (photonic cavity) to demonstrating high-speed measurements on single molecules (ferritin), followed by detailed kinetic analysis using HMMs and PSD fitting to map out the underlying energy landscape and its tunability.
why_interesting: This work directly applies advanced optical sensing techniques to study molecular dynamics, which is a core area of AMO physics. The use of cavity resonance shifts as a highly sensitive probe for local changes in polarizability mimics quantum coupling measurements, making it relevant to open quantum systems characterization.

A tapered fibre is bonded to individual cavities, before cleaving from the chip for measurement in solution. FIG. 2. Ferritin monolayer formation via adsorption onto the cavity surface. a, Signal measured prior to the addition of proteins to the solution (150 mM NaCl). b, After the addition of proteins (1 nM apo-ferritin), a gradual shift in cavity resonance is observed as a monolayer of the protein is formed across the nanobeam surface. The inset highlights a single ferritin adsorption event within the slot region. c, Stabilized signal observed after several minutes. Once the monolayer has been formed and stabilised, the laser is retuned to the side of the cavity resonance for subsequent measurements.

FIG. 3. Optical tracking of fast ferritin motions. a, Recording of a single holoferritin attaching to a holoferritin monolayer. Compared with direct binding to the cavity, these events are rare, transient, and feature an increase in signal fluctuations. b, The corresponding power spectral density of post-binding fluctuations (blue), compared with the bare device signal (grey). The protein signal is fit to a Lorentzian model (black dashed), and the baseline noise to a linear curve (grey dashed). c, The wavelength shift histogram is plot as a relative potential landscape, displaying a bimodal distribution. A 10 Hz high-pass filter is applied to remove measurement drift.

FIG. 4. Analysis of stepping dynamics in ferritin. a, Short time scale view of single-holoferritin signal from Fig. 3a, displaying stepping between an ‘upper’ and ‘lower’ state. b, Forty different upward transition of holoferritin in a, with the blue solid curve showing their average. c, Histograms of the wavelength shift for holoferritin at low NaCl (4 mM, top), holoferritin and apoferritin at medium NaCl (10 mM, middle), and apoferritin at high NaCl (150 mM, bottom). A 10 Hz high-pass filter is applied before data analysis to remove measurement drift.
